Side effectsDrugs (probably responsible)Management
Major
Generalized severe skin rash with or without itchingIsoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and EthambutolStop anti-TB drugs and refer. Re-challenge once stable, starting with the least likely causative agent. Give antihistamines to manage pruritis
Deafness (no wax on otoscopy)Injectable *Stop Injectable and refer
Dizziness (vertigo and nystagmus)Injectable *Stop Injectable and refer
Jaundice (other causes excluded), hepatitisPyrazinamide, INH, RifampicinStop anti-TB drugs and refer Re-challenge once stable starting with the least hepatotoxic agent
Confusion (suspect drug-induced acute liver failure if there is jaundice)Most anti-TB drugsStop anti-TB drugs and refer
Visual impairment (other causes excluded)EthambutolStop Ethambutol and refer
Shock, purpura, acute renal failureRifampicinStop Rifampicin and refer
Decreased urine output (acute renal failure)Injectable *Stop Injectable and refer Adjust the doses of other renally-excreted drugs e.g. Ethambutol
Minor
Anorexia, nausea, abdominal painPyrazinamide, Rifampicin, INHGive drugs with small meals or just before bedtime and advise the patient to swallow pills slowly with small sips of water. If the symptoms persist or worsen, or there is protracted vomiting or any sign of bleeding, consider the side-effect to be major and refer to the Clinician urgently.
Joint painsPyrazinamideAspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or Paracetamol.
Major
Burning, numbness or tingling sensation in the hands or feetINHGive Pyridoxine 50-75mg daily Can go up to 100mg. Refer if no improvement or grade 3 or 4 neuropathy.
DrowsinessINHReassure the patient. Give drugs before bedtime.
Orange/red urineRifampicinReassure patient. Patients should be informed about the urine change when initiating TB treatment.
Flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, malaise, headache, bone pain)Intermittent dosing of RifampicinReassure patient. When starting TB treatment, patients should be informed about the possibility of such occurring and that it is normal.

Table 41: Guide to performing anti-TB drug challenge and re-introduction (Drug, Likelihood of causing
a reaction, Challenge doses)

Drugs are reintroduced one at a time starting with the drug least likely to cause the reaction. If the drug responsible is pyrazinamide, ethambutol or streptomycin, resume TB treatment without the offending drug and, if possible, replace it; the regimen may need to be extended.

Potassium level (mEq/L)Quantity of KCl (1 mEq IV = 1 mmol IV; 8 mEq = 600 mg tablet)When to do the next control (sooner if the patient has vomiting or diarrhoea)
4.0 or moreNoneMonthly

Every Slow-K 600 mg tablet contains 8 mEq of K; every magnesium tablet contains 150 mg magnesium oxide. Potassium IV supplementation should NOT exceed 20 mmol/hr of KCl (usual 40 mmol in 1 L NaCl 0.9%, maximum 60 mmol/L). Magnesium IV: maximum 5 g MgSO4 in 1 L NaCl 0.9% or dextrose 5%, not faster than 150 mg/min; if not an emergency 2 g in 100 ml over 1-2 hours or 4 g in 250 ml over 2-4 hours. Amiloride or spironolactone are useful in resistant cases.

Note: Every Slow-K 600 mg tablet contains 8 mEq of K; every magnesium tablet contains 150 mg magnesium oxide. Potassium IV supplementation should NOT exceed 20 mmol/hr of KCl (usual 40 mmol in 1 L NaCl 0.9%, maximum 60 mmol/L). Magnesium IV: maximum 5 g MgSO4 in 1 L NaCl 0.9% or dextrose 5%, not faster than 150 mg/min; if not an emergency 2 g in 100 ml over 1-2 hours or 4 g in 250 ml over 2-4 hours. Amiloride or spironolactone are useful in resistant cases.

Source: Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Drug-resistant Tuberculosis, Emergency update 2008, WHO/HTM/TB/2008.402.

Every Slow-K 600 mg tablet contains 8 mEq of K; every magnesium tablet contains 150 mg magnesium oxide. Potassium IV supplementation should NOT exceed 20 mmol/hr of KCl (usual 40 mmol in 1 L NaCl 0.9%, maximum 60 mmol/L). Magnesium IV: maximum 5 g MgSO4 in 1 L NaCl 0.9% or dextrose 5%, not faster than 150 mg/min; if not an emergency 2 g in 100 ml over 1-2 hours or 4 g in 250 ml over 2-4 hours. Amiloride or spironolactone are useful in resistant cases.

Points to check in the source:
  • Grade 1 is printed as '45 - 480 msec' (presumably 451-480 msec); grade 4 as '> 501 msec or 60 msec change' (usually >500 msec or >60 msec increase from baseline).

PDF page

New: flowchart

Items: If on multiple QtcF prolonging drugs, stop ancillary drugs first. Then stop MFX if receiving this drug. If QTcF prolongation persists, then stop CFZ. If CTcF prolongation persists, then stop BDQ.
- Causative Medications: BDQ, CFZ, MFX, DLM, LFX -> QTcF prolongation: Signs and symptoms include palpitations, syncope/fainting, dizziness
- Monitor for QTcF prolongation by checking an ECG at baseline, week 2 and monthly until month 6 or anytime if there are symptoms -> QTcF prolongation: Signs and symptoms include palpitations, syncope/fainting, dizziness
- QTcF prolongation: Signs and symptoms include palpitations, syncope/fainting, dizziness -> Assess ECG. If QtcF is prolonged, repeat ECG. Consider other possible causes including low potassium, malnutrition, hypothyroidism or other medications. Consider checking and replacing potassium if vomiting or diarrhea.
- Assess ECG. If QtcF is prolonged, repeat ECG. Consider other possible causes including low potassium, malnutrition, hypothyroidism or other medications. Consider checking and replacing potassium if vomiting or diarrhea. -> Assess severity and manage
- Assess severity and manage -> Mild/Grade 1: *45 - 480 msec* Monitor closely, weekly ECG until QTcF < grade or baseline; correct electrolytes or other causes as needed; Moderate/Grade 2: *> 480 - 500 msec* Monitor closely, weekly ECG until QTcF < grade or baseline; correct electrolytes or other causes as needed; Severe/Grade 3: *> 500 msec* Stop the suspected causative drug(s); hospitalize and correct electrolytes or other underlying causes as needed; Life-threatening/Grade 4: *> 501 msec or 60 msec change from baseline and one of the following:* Torsades de pointers polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, or signs/symptoms or serious arrhythmia. Stop the suspected causative drugs; hospitalize and correct electrolytes or other underlying causes

Figure 31. Management of liver function abnormalities on TB drugs (PZA, INH, BDQ, CFZ, Eto, PAS): LFT monitoring, grades 1-4 by ULN, stop and reintroduce drugs, liver-sparing regimen

Check: {"new_not_in_pdf_text": [], "new_not_in_old_chunks": [], "old_not_in_new": ["31"]} (compared with the PDF text layer and the old chunks)

  • Grade 3 reads '> 5 to 10 ULN or any asymptomatic elevations' – probably 'symptomatic' (drug-induced liver injury is usually ALT >3×ULN with symptoms or >5×ULN without).

PDF page

New: flowchart

- Causative Medications: PZA, INH, BDQ, CFZ, Eto, PAS -> Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching
- Monitor elevated liver function tests at baseline and monthly for the first six months of treatment and anytime if there are symptoms -> Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching
- Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching -> Assess for other causes. These include alcohol use, use of traditional medicines/ herbs, viral hepatitis and TB itself
- Assess for other causes. These include alcohol use, use of traditional medicines/ herbs, viral hepatitis and TB itself -> Assess severity and manage
- Assess severity and manage -> Mild/Grade 1: >1 to 2.5 times ULN and asymptomatic Continue treatment and follow until return to baseline or stabilization of AST/ALT elevation; Moderate/Grade 2: >2.5 to 5 times ULN and asymptomatic Continue treatment and follow until return to baseline or stabilization of AST/ALT elevation; Severe/Grade 3: > 5 to 10 ULN or any asymptomatic elevations Stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly; reintroduce drugs after toxicity is resolved; Life-threatening/Grade 4: > 10 time ULN regardless of symptoms Stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly; reintroduce drugs after toxicity is resolved
Liver-sparing regimen drugs: EMB, DLM, CS, amikacin (with caution) and likely the FQs. People with underlying liver disease, heavy alcohol use or viral hepatitis should start a modified shorter regimen that includes CS and does NOT include INH or PZA.

Diagram: Management of Liver Function Abnormalities (section: Figure 31: Management of Liver Function Abnormalities)

- Causative Medications: PZA, INH, BDQ, CFZ, Eto, PAS -> Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching

- Monitor elevated liver function tests at baseline and monthly for the first six months of treatment and anytime if there are symptoms -> Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching

- Liver Function Abnormalities: Liver function test abnormalities can present asymptomaticaly or with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice/icterus, itching -> Assess for other causes. These include alcohol use, use of traditional medicines/ herbs, viral hepatitis and TB itself

- Assess for other causes. These include alcohol use, use of traditional medicines/ herbs, viral hepatitis and TB itself -> Assess severity and manage

- Assess severity and manage -> Mild/Grade 1: >1 to 2.5 times ULN and asymptomatic Continue treatment and follow until return to baseline or stabilization of AST/ALT elevation; Moderate/Grade 2: >2.5 to 5 times ULN and asymptomatic Continue treatment and follow until return to baseline or stabilization of AST/ALT elevation; Severe/Grade 3: > 5 to 10 ULN or any asymptomatic elevations Stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly; reintroduce drugs after toxicity is resolved; Life-threatening/Grade 4: > 10 time ULN regardless of symptoms Stop all drugs, measure LFTs weekly; reintroduce drugs after toxicity is resolved

Drugs that should be used in a “liver sparing regimen” include EMB, DLM, CS, amikacin (with caution) and likely the FQs.

Of notes, persons with underlying liver disease, heavy alcohol use or viral hepatitis should be started on a modified shorter regimen that includes CS and does NOT include INH or PZA

Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB (Patient Category, When to start ART)
Patient CategoryWhen to start ART
Among PLHIV who are presumptive for TBInitiate ART while rapidly investigating for TB, with close follow-up within seven days to initiate TB treatment if TB is confirmed
Among PLHIV on ART and diagnosed with TBContinue ART and initiate anti-TB treatment as soon as diagnosed, may need to adjust ART regimen/dosage if required
For newly diagnosed PLHIV/returnees who also have been diagnosed with TBInitiate ART as soon as possible preferably within 2 weeks of initiating tuberculosis treatment (including same-day anti-TB and ART treatment if clinically stable) regardless of immune status
Patients with TB meningitisDelay ART to 4 weeks post-initiation of anti-TB treatment

Table 45: Recommended periods to start ART in PLHIV with presumptive TB and confirmed TB (Patient Category, When to start ART).
Among PLHIV who are presumptive for TB: When to start ART: Initiate ART while rapidly investigating for TB, with close follow-up within seven days to initiate TB treatment if TB is confirmed.
Among PLHIV on ART and diagnosed with TB: When to start ART: Continue ART and initiate anti-TB treatment as soon as diagnosed, may need to adjust ART regimen/dosage if required.
For newly diagnosed PLHIV/returnees who also have been diagnosed with TB: When to start ART: Initiate ART as soon as possible preferably within 2 weeks of initiating tuberculosis treatment (including same-day anti-TB and ART treatment if clinically stable) regardless of immune status.
Patients with TB meningitis: When to start ART: Delay ART to 4 weeks post-initiation of anti-TB treatment.

Table 46: Recommended Adult ART Regimens for TB/HIV Co-infected patients (Client Category, Recommended ART regimen, Comments)
Client categoryRecommended ART regimenComments
Clients already on TB treatment presenting for ART initiationTDF (300 mg)/3TC (300 mg) once daily + DTG (50 mg twice daily)- Start ART as soon as possible with increased DTG dosing of 50 mg twice daily<br/>- Return to standard DTG dosing 50 mg once daily two weeks after the completion of TB treatment
Clients developing TB while on a DTG-based ART regimenIncrease DTG dose to 50 mg twice dailyClients must return to DTG 50 mg once daily 2 weeks after completing TB treatment.
Developing DS-TB while on an EFV-based ART regimenTDF/3TC+EFV 400 mg (once daily)- Check VL at the end of treatment. If VL is undetectable, the client can be transitioned to a once-daily FDC of TDF+3TC+DTG two weeks after completion of TB treatment<br/>- If VL is detectable, immediately switch to second line and continue adherence support (refer to the ART section)
Developing DS-TB while on a protease inhibitor (PI)-based ART regimenConsult an experienced HIV clinician or snapthirdline@mohcoag.org before choosing these options:<br/>TB patient on LPV/r:<br/>- Super-boost LPV/r to 400 mg/400 mg by adding 300 mg ritonavir, and continue until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment<br/>- Double-dose LPV/r to 800 mg/200 mg twice daily (double dosing is only for clients >10 years of age) and continue until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment<br/>- If evidence of VL suppression in the past 3-6 months, switch to a DTG-based second-line regimen and continue twice-daily DTG until 2 weeks after completion of TB treatment<br/>TB patient on ATV/r or DRV/r:<br/>- Do not combine with rifampicin<br/>- Change to DTG twice daily if DTG-naive, or LPV/r with adjustments as above if DTG-experienced<br/>Patients who may be failing ART:<br/>- Follow guidance on managing treatment failure
For clients with multidrug-resistant TB
EFV and bedaquiline (BDQ)- EFV should not be used with BDQ.<br/>- EFV induces CYP3A activity and co-administration with BDQ may result in reduced BDQ exposure and loss of BDQ activity.<br/>- DTG is the preferred INSTI for clients receiving BDQ.
Delamanid (DLM) and ARVs- DLM is generally considered safe to administer with ART.<br/>- Evidence shows safety with EFV, TDF and LPV/r.<br/>- No LPV/r dose adjustment is needed for TB patients on DLM. No long-term studies have been done on drug-drug interactions between DLM and ARVs. DTG is the preferred INSTI for clients receiving DLM.
For all clients, maintain the same NRTI backbone provided no dose adjustment is necessary and the client is virally suppressed.

Points to check in the source:
  • The 'DTG and all TB treatments' row says the preference is to keep clients on TDF+3TC+EFV during TB treatment, which conflicts with Table 46 (increase DTG to 50 mg twice daily during rifampicin-based treatment, the current WHO approach).
  • Rifampicin and the oral contraceptive pill: 'receive a pill containing a higher dose of oestrogen (50 μg)' – current guidance (WHO MEC) is to use another method (e.g. DMPA, IUD) rather than a higher-dose pill.

Table 47: TB treatment/ART Drug Interactions (Drug combination, Considerations)
Drug combinationConsiderations
Rifampicin and (LPV/r)- LPV/r can be used with Rifampicin - Super boost the LPV/r (1:1 lopinavir and ritonavir) by adding ritonavir. - Closely monitor the client for toxicity (especially gastrointestinal intolerance) and virological failure
Rifampicin and Oral Contraceptive Pill- Oral contraceptive pills may not be effective when administered with RIF. - Women of childbearing age should either receive a contraceptive pill containing a higher dose of oestrogen (50μg) or use another form of contraception (e.g., medroxyprogesterone). - Emphasize concomitant condom use during this period
DTG and all TB treatments- Preference is for clients to be maintained on a fixed dose combination of TDF+3TC+EFV for the duration of TB treatment. - Check VL at the end of TB treatment. If the VL is undetectable: the client can be transitioned to a once-daily FDC of TDF+3TC+DTG two weeks after completion of TB treatment. If the VL is detectable, immediately switch to the second line and continue adherence support. - If the client is on a DTG regimen, the DTG does need to be given as 50mg twice daily until at least 2 weeks after the client has completed TB treatment. This may increase the occurrence of DTG side effects.

< 10 kgNot on ARTLPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ (recommended if ritonavir is not available) or NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵

< 10 kgNVPContinue NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵

Guiding principles: always immediately check viral load and CD4 in a patient on ART who is diagnosed with TB; if VL is detectable avoid a one-drug change and manage as treatment failure considering ART/ATT interactions; consider ART and PMTCT history; NRTI companion drugs per HIV guidelines (weight, comorbidities, prior NRTI exposure); consult TB/HIV experts (NTCP, ENAP, partners) for questions and patients failing second-line ART or a PI.

Note: Guiding principles: always immediately check viral load and CD4 in a patient on ART who is diagnosed with TB; if VL is detectable avoid a one-drug change and manage as treatment failure considering ART/ATT interactions; consider ART and PMTCT history; NRTI companion drugs per HIV guidelines (weight, comorbidities, prior NRTI exposure); consult TB/HIV experts (NTCP, ENAP, partners) for questions and patients failing second-line ART or a PI.

1. See Dosing Table **** for 1:1 LPV/r (ritonavir solution and capsules) [as printed]. 2. NEVER continue ABC-3TC-AZT or an NVP-based regimen for more than 2 weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 3. Consider ABC-3TC-AZT or NVP if intolerant to LPV/r. 4. Avoid NVP if prior exposure to PMTCT or ART. 5. Start at full dose and increase the dose to 200 mg/m²/dose if formulation allows when co-administered with rifampicin. 6. LPV/r can be administered as a double dose instead of 1:1 in children swallowing LPV/r tablets, reduced to standard dosing 2 weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 7. DTG must be given twice daily while on TB treatment and continued twice daily for two weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 8. NVP can be continued during TB treatment instead of EFV if intolerance or cannot swallow EFV. 9. Plan to change to DTG from EFV following completion of TB treatment (two weeks after rifampicin is stopped) if viral load is undetectable.

Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children – patients initiating ART while on TB treatment > < 10 kg: Current ART regimen: Not on ART; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ (recommended if ritonavir is not available) or NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵.
Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children – patients initiating ART while on TB treatment > 10-20 kg: Current ART regimen: Not on ART; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): EFV (recommended) or LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³.
Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children – patients initiating ART while on TB treatment > > 20 kg: Current ART regimen: Not on ART; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): DTG ⁷ twice daily (recommended).
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > < 10 kg: Current ART regimen: NVP; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): Continue NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵.
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > < 10 kg: Current ART regimen: LPV/r; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³ (recommended if ritonavir not available) or NVP ² ³ ⁴ ⁵.
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > 10-20 kg: Current ART regimen: NVP or EFV; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): EFV ⁸.
National Integrated TB Management Guidelines (2025) | 10.6 Management of TB in children living with HIV > Table 50: TB/HIV Simplified Treatment Table (page 201)

Table 50: TB/HIV Simplified Treatment Table (Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children) (part 2 of 3).
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > 10-20 kg: Current ART regimen: LPV/r (1st-line ART); Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ¹ ⁶ (recommended) or EFV (recommended if VL undetectable in the last 6 months) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³.
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > 10-20 kg: Current ART regimen: LPV/r (2nd-line treatment); Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): LPV/r with 1:1 ritonavir boosting ⁶ (recommended) or ABC-3TC-AZT ² ³.
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > > 20 kg: Current ART regimen: NVP or EFV; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): EFV ⁸ ⁹.
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > > 20 kg: Current ART regimen: ATV/r or LPV/r (1st or 2nd line); Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): LPV/r double dose ⁶ or DTG ⁷ twice daily (if VL confirmed undetectable at TB treatment initiation).
Modifications to ART when initiating TB treatment in patients on ART > > 20 kg: Current ART regimen: DTG; Initial regimen / suggested modification (NRTIs based on HIV guidelines): Twice-daily DTG ⁷.
National Integrated TB Management Guidelines (2025) | 10.6 Management of TB in children living with HIV > Table 50: TB/HIV Simplified Treatment Table (page 201)

Table 50: TB/HIV Simplified Treatment Table (Treatment of HIV-associated TB in children) (part 3 of 3).
Guiding principles: always immediately check viral load and CD4 in a patient on ART who is diagnosed with TB; if VL is detectable avoid a one-drug change and manage as treatment failure considering ART/ATT interactions; consider ART and PMTCT history; NRTI companion drugs per HIV guidelines (weight, comorbidities, prior NRTI exposure); consult TB/HIV experts (NTCP, ENAP, partners) for questions and patients failing second-line ART or a PI.
1. See Dosing Table **** for 1:1 LPV/r (ritonavir solution and capsules) [as printed]. 2. NEVER continue ABC-3TC-AZT or an NVP-based regimen for more than 2 weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 3. Consider ABC-3TC-AZT or NVP if intolerant to LPV/r. 4. Avoid NVP if prior exposure to PMTCT or ART. 5. Start at full dose and increase the dose to 200 mg/m²/dose if formulation allows when co-administered with rifampicin. 6. LPV/r can be administered as a double dose instead of 1:1 in children swallowing LPV/r tablets, reduced to standard dosing 2 weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 7. DTG must be given twice daily while on TB treatment and continued twice daily for two weeks after rifampicin is discontinued. 8. NVP can be continued during TB treatment instead of EFV if intolerance or cannot swallow EFV. 9. Plan to change to DTG from EFV following completion of TB treatment (two weeks after rifampicin is stopped) if viral load is undetectable.

New: flowchart

- Household TB contacts. Other Risk Groups* -> Symptom based screening (CXR if available)
- Symptom based screening (CXR if available) -> Positive (S/S and/or CXC); *Negative (S/S and/or CXC)
- Positive (S/S and/or CXC) -> Evaluate for TB/DR-TB
- Evaluate for TB/DR-TB -> TB/DR-TB disease; No TB
- TB/DR-TB disease -> Treat for TB/DR-TB
- No TB -> Start TPT
- *Negative (S/S and/or CXC) -> Perform TBI Test; TBI test unavailable and household contact
- Perform TBI Test -> Positive; Negative; Indeterminate
- Positive -> Start TPT
- Negative -> No TPT
- Indeterminate -> No TPT
- TBI test unavailable and household contact -> Start TPT
Neither CXR nor a TB infection (TBI) test is mandatory to decide to start TPT. Other risk groups: silicosis, immunosuppressive drugs (long steroid therapy, cancer chemotherapy), anti-TNF treatment, transplantation (including candidates), health care workers and offenders.

Points to check in the source:
  • 1HP row lists 'Rifapentine 30 mg tab' (2 tablets); the 1HP rifapentine dose is 600 mg daily, i.e. 2 × 300 mg tablets.
  • The last weight column is printed '< 50 kg' after 45-49.9 kg (presumably ≥50 kg); the first two columns are '3-5.9 kg (> 3 months)' and '3-5.9 kg (≥ 3 months)', so the under-3-months band is missing.
  • 1HP footnote reads 'for individuals aged < 13 years'; 1HP is recommended for people aged ≥13 years (Table 58 says ≥12 years).
  • Lfx 250 mg tab has no dose for 20-24.9 kg ('–') although the bands either side are covered.
  • Footnote d (rifapentine 15 mg/mL solution) is attached to the levofloxacin 250 mg suspension volumes.

Table 58: TPT regimens and dosing for people living with HIV: 3HP (preferred, ≥12 years and ≥25 kg), 1HP alternative, 6H for children <14 years or <30 kg and pregnant women, isoniazid mg/kg by age, vitamin B6
Population groupPreferred regimenAlternative regimen
Individuals ≥12 years and ≥25 kg3HP*: weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months (rifapentine 300 mg/isoniazid 300 mg per tablet, 12 doses) – 3 tablets weekly plus 25 or 50 mg [as printed] plus vitamin B6 weekly1HP (when available): daily isoniazid plus rifapentine for 1 month. Dosage: 300 mg isoniazid and 600 mg rifapentine daily plus 25 mg vitamin B6 daily
Children <14 years or weight <30 kg6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily. Isoniazid dosing: <10 years 10 mg/kg/day; >10 years 5 mg/kg/day3HP/1HP may be used for ≥2 years old when a child-friendly formula is available.
Pregnant women6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily (dosing 5 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg/day). PNP prophylaxis for INH-containing regimen: vitamin B6 10-25 mg/day—
3HP is not recommended for PLHIV taking antiretrovirals with clinically significant or unknown drug interactions with rifapentine, or for people presumed infected with isoniazid- or rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis. In infants receiving NVP for prevention of mother-to-child transmission, 6H should be the preferred regimen; caregivers of exposed infants who complete PMTCT should be told that if the infant becomes HIV positive, TPT may need to change from 3HR to avoid drug interactions.

National Integrated TB Management Guidelines (2025) | Chapter 11: Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment > 11.8 TPT Regimens and Dosing > Table 58: TPT Regimens and Dosing for PLHIV (page 217)

Table 58: TPT regimens and dosing for people living with HIV: 3HP (preferred, ≥12 years and ≥25 kg), 1HP alternative, 6H for children <14 years or <30 kg and pregnant women, isoniazid mg/kg by age, vitamin B6.
Individuals ≥12 years and ≥25 kg: Preferred regimen: 3HP*: weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months (rifapentine 300 mg/isoniazid 300 mg per tablet, 12 doses) – 3 tablets weekly plus 25 or 50 mg [as printed] plus vitamin B6 weekly; Alternative regimen: 1HP (when available): daily isoniazid plus rifapentine for 1 month. Dosage: 300 mg isoniazid and 600 mg rifapentine daily plus 25 mg vitamin B6 daily.
Children <14 years or weight <30 kg: Preferred regimen: 6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily. Isoniazid dosing: <10 years 10 mg/kg/day; >10 years 5 mg/kg/day; Alternative regimen: 3HP/1HP may be used for ≥2 years old when a child-friendly formula is available.
Pregnant women: Preferred regimen: 6H: 6 months of daily isoniazid plus vitamin B6 25 mg daily (dosing 5 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg/day). PNP prophylaxis for INH-containing regimen: vitamin B6 10-25 mg/day; Alternative regimen: —.
3HP is not recommended for PLHIV taking antiretrovirals with clinically significant or unknown drug interactions with rifapentine, or for people presumed infected with isoniazid- or rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis. In infants receiving NVP for prevention of mother-to-child transmission, 6H should be the preferred regimen; caregivers of exposed infants who complete PMTCT should be told that if the infant becomes HIV positive, TPT may need to change from 3HR to avoid drug interactions.

Table 59: Documented adverse events with drug used for TPT (Adverse event, Responsible drug, Management)
Adverse eventResponsible drugManagement
Flu-like signs and symptomsRifapentine, rifampicin• Advise to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of water and juice.<br/>• Prescribe Paracetamol which may be taken every 4 to 6 hours. Leave at least 4 hours between doses. (Dosage 500mg tab for adults, for children 3 months- 6 years 120mg/5ml suspension, children 6 years of age and adults 250mg/5ml suspension.)<br/>• If severe and not tolerated to 3HP/3HR regimen, consider switching to an alternate regimen (6H)
Nausea and<br/>vomitingRifapentine, rifampicin,<br/>isoniazid• Prescribe 10 mg of metoclopramide bid (twice a day) or<br/>tid.<br/>• Advise patients to stay hydrated by drinking plenty of<br/>water and juice.<br/>• Avoid spicy and greasy foods.<br/>• Prescribe oral rehydration solution if mild dehydration is<br/>present.
HepatotoxicityMore with INH than<br/>rifapentine and rifampicin)• If people on TPT have signs and symptoms of<br/>hepatotoxicity, perform LFT.<br/>• If aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and/or alanine<br/>aminotransferase (ALT) are >3 but <5 times upper limit of<br/>normal (ULN) without signs and symptoms of hepatitis,<br/>continue TPT and repeat AST and ALT weekly.<br/>• If AST and/or ALT >3 times ULN with signs and symptoms<br/>of hepatitis or if AST and/or ALT >5 times ULN with or<br/>without signs and symptoms of hepatitis, stop TPT and do<br/>not reintroduce.
Peripheral<br/>neuropathyIsoniazid• Use brief peripheral neuropathy scoring system<br/>(BPNS) to screen and assess the severity of peripheral<br/>neuropathy.<br/>• If mild: give 100 to 150 mg of pyridoxine in adults and 50<br/>mg in children.<br/>• If not better or worsened with an increased pyridoxine<br/>dose, stop the H-containing regimen and consider<br/>switching to 4R.
Skin<br/>hypersensitivity<br/>reactionRifampicin, Rifapentine,<br/>Isoniazid• If itchiness and localized mild rashes occur, give calamine<br/>lotion or steroid cream to apply bid on the affected area;<br/>chlorpheniramine 8 mg tid or bid orally may be given.<br/>• If itchiness, generalized rashes, or swelling of oral or nasal<br/>mucosa with or without fever, withhold TPT.<br/>• For mild or moderate hypersensitivity reaction,<br/>desensitization may be attempted with a low dose rechallenge once the rash resolves starting with isoniazid<br/>alone at 1/6 normal dose on day 1, then full dose on day<br/>2 and subsequently monitoring closely, especially on the<br/>completion of antihistamines (at least weekly to 2-weekly<br/>for the first month then monthly).<br/>• If a rash does not recur, continue isoniazid monotherapy<br/>ensuring that the client gets a total of 180 doses.<br/>If rash recurs, do not rechallenge with isoniazid.<br/>Alternative regimen 4R may be considered by re-introduction with a low dose (1/6 of the dose) on day 1 and then a full dose on day 2.<br/>• If desensitization cannot be performed, an alternative regimen (e.g. 4R or 6H) may be considered<br/>• Never reintroduce after severe hypersensitivity reaction or Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Orange-red discoloration of body fluid (tear, saliva, urine, milk, urine)Rifampicin, rifapentine• Reassure that it is just the staining from a drug in the regimen and is harmless. Advice to continue TPT.
Any occurrence of TB signs and symptoms• Investigate for active TB disease or other diseases.<br/>• If there is no active TB disease, continue TPT.<br/>• If active TB disease, stop TPT and provide DS-TB or DR-TB treatment, as appropriate.

for the first month then monthly).
• If a rash does not recur, continue isoniazid monotherapy
ensuring that the client gets a total of 180 doses.
If rash recurs, do not rechallenge with isoniazid.
Alternative regimen 4R may be considered by re-introduction with a low dose (1/6 of the dose) on day 1 and then a full dose on day 2.
• If desensitization cannot be performed, an alternative regimen (e.g. 4R or 6H) may be considered
• Never reintroduce after severe hypersensitivity reaction or Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Orange-red discoloration of body fluid (tear, saliva, urine, milk, urine)Rifampicin, rifapentine• Reassure that it is just the staining from a drug in the regimen and is harmless. Advice to continue TPT.
Any occurrence of TB signs and symptoms• Investigate for active TB disease or other diseases.
• If there is no active TB disease, continue TPT.
• If active TB disease, stop TPT and provide DS-TB or DR-TB treatment, as appropriate.

Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose (TPT regimen, Duration of treatment interruption, Next Steps)
TPT regimenDuration of treatment interruptionNext Steps
3HP1 weekly dose missed<br/>More than 1 weekly doses missedIf the missed dose is remembered within the next 2 days, continue to take the remaining doses according to the original schedule. If the missed dose is remembered > 2 days later, take the missed dose immediately, and change the schedule for weekly intake to the day the missed dose was taken, until treatment completion. This will avoid 2 weekly doses being taken fewer than 4 days apart.<br/>If treatment interruption occurred after at least 9 doses were taken within 12 weeks of starting, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 112 days. If ≥ 4 weekly doses are missed, consider restarting the full TPT course. If an individual has difficulty adhering to a weekly routine, consider dis continuing 3HP and offering an alternative regimen with daily dosing.
1HPLess than 7 doses missed<br/>More than 7 doses missedContinue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT)<br/>If < 7 consecutive doses were missed, consider restarting the complete course of the 1HP regimen. If > 7 doses were missed intermittently, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT)
3HR, 4R, 6H, 6LfxLess than 2 weeks<br/>More than 2 weeksResume TPT and add the number of missed doses to the total treatment duration.<br/>Do not change the scheduled date of the next follow-up visit, but postpone the last follow-up visit by the number of extra days to compensate for missed doses. For example, if a child on 3HR misses 3 days of treatment, continue TPT for a total of 3 months + 3 days from the date of start.<br/>If treatment interruption occurs after more than 80% of doses in the regimen have been taken, continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. If less than 80% of doses in the regimen were taken, and the treatment course can still be completed within the expected treatment duration + 33% additional time, continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. For example, if an adult on 6H had taken only 120 doses by month 6, the remaining 62 doses can be taken in the next 2 months, without exceeding the 239-day limit. If < 80% of doses in the regimen were taken, and the treatment course cannot be completed within the expected time, consider restarting the full TPT course. A shorter regimen would be preferable.

Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose (TPT regimen, Duration of treatment interruption, Next Steps)

Table 62: Management of TPT interruption or missed dose

TPT regimenDuration of treatment interruptionNext Steps
3HP1 weekly dose missed
More than 1 weekly doses missed		If the missed dose is remembered within the next 2 days, continue to take the remaining doses according to the original schedule. If the missed dose is remembered > 2 days later, take the missed dose immediately, and change the schedule for weekly intake to the day the missed dose was taken, until treatment completion. This will avoid 2 weekly doses being taken fewer than 4 days apart.
If treatment interruption occurred after at least 9 doses were taken within 12 weeks of starting, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 112 days. If ≥ 4 weekly doses are missed, consider restarting the full TPT course. If an individual has difficulty adhering to a weekly routine, consider dis continuing 3HP and offering an alternative regimen with daily dosing.
1HPLess than 7 doses missed
More than 7 doses missed		Continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT)
If < 7 consecutive doses were missed, consider restarting the complete course of the 1HP regimen. If > 7 doses were missed intermittently, continue and complete the remaining doses, thus prolonging the total treatment duration to a maximum of 6 weeks (42 days from starting TPT)
3HR, 4R, 6H, 6LfxLess than 2 weeks
More than 2 weeks		Resume TPT and add the number of missed doses to the total treatment duration.
Do not change the scheduled date of the next follow-up visit, but postpone the last follow-up visit by the number of extra days to compensate for missed doses. For example, if a child on 3HR misses 3 days of treatment, continue TPT for a total of 3 months + 3 days from the date of start.
If treatment interruption occurs after more than 80% of doses in the regimen have been taken, continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. If less than 80% of doses in the regimen were taken, and the treatment course can still be completed within the expected treatment duration + 33% additional time, continue and complete the remaining treatment as per the original plan. For example, if an adult on 6H had taken only 120 doses by month 6, the remaining 62 doses can be taken in the next 2 months, without exceeding the 239-day limit. If < 80% of doses in the regimen were taken, and the treatment course cannot be completed within the expected time, consider restarting the full TPT course. A shorter regimen would be preferable.

  • The chart annotation says a 2-year-old girl weighing 14 kg is at -2 Z score; on the WHO girls' weight-for-age standard 14 kg at 24 months is above +1 SD (the -2 SD line is about 9 kg). The example appears wrong.
